title: Why You Shouldn't Pull Students Aside To Discuss Their Misbehavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the near-universal practice of pulling a misbehaving student aside for a one-on-one talk, calling it a mistake that increases rather than decreases future misbehavior. He gives three reasons: it undermines student agency by short-circuiting the reflection process that actually changes behavior when students are left to think for themselves; it causes resentment, since students experience the meeting as an added, uncomfortable consequence rather than a caring conversation, especially if any lecturing or forced apology occurs; and it contradicts the teacher's word, since anything beyond the stated classroom management plan reads to students as a broken promise and a form of revenge, which the rest of the class also perceives. His alternative is to trust the classroom management plan alone to do its job and to save the teacher's time for what matters most: instruction, since time on task is what actually builds students' competence, self-worth, and long-term distance from misbehavior.
points: Pulling a student aside for a one-on-one chat about misbehavior undermines the self-directed reflection that actually changes behavior.
Students experience being pulled aside as an added, uncomfortable consequence, not a caring conversation, especially if any lecturing occurs.
Adding anything beyond the stated classroom management plan reads to students as a broken promise, and the rest of the class notices and assumes revenge.
Trust the classroom management plan alone to do the work; you don't have time to talk individually to every student who breaks a rule.
Academic competence, built through protected time on task, is framed as the best thing a teacher can do for students' future and their distance from misbehavior.
quotes: Pulling a student aside for a chat about their misbehavior is a common practice. Intuitively, it would appear to make sense.
When you tell students what to think or what they should have done or request assurances from them, you undermine their inclination to choose of their own volition to improve their behavior.
One-on-one meetings are also incredibly uncomfortable for students. What you may see as a simple discussion, they view as an additional consequence.
Students see this as a lie and betrayal. You may not regard it this way, if it even occurs to you.

You must be able to follow your classroom management plan quickly and without interruption so you can get back to the business of teaching and learning. Time on task is everything to academic progress.

Weighted down with purpose, agency, responsibility, and competence, and empowered by the freedom to think and then choose behavior that is best for them and their classmates, they become mature, independent, tenacious.
